prompt.context: Our client, Arbor Housing, is a leading provider of short term and temporary corporate housing. Profits have remained steady the past few years, and Arbor was recently purchased by a private equity firm that has brought in new management. The new CEO has been charged with increasing sales in order to meet management's growth targets for the next few years.
prompt.question: What can Arbor Housing do to increase revenues, while remaining profitable?

clarifying_info.a: Corporate housing are fully furnished short term or temporary apartment-style accommodations.

clarifying_info.q: Does Arbor own or lease its locations?
clarifying_info.a: Arbor owns many of their locations and leases vacancies in other apartment buildings. Assume that capacity needed for growth can be leased and major investment is not required.
This is a US-based case; Arbor has locations in all major cities.
Arbor competes against hotels and apartment buildings that offer short-term leases. For this case, ignore the effect of competitors that also offer corporate housing.
Nights Stayed is a common metric used as a proxy for revenue.

exhibits.title: Annual nights stayed (MM) 2006-2010
exhibits.shows: A grouped bar chart showing annual nights stayed (in millions) from 2006 to 2010, broken out by four industry segments: Professional Services (includes Consulting, Accounting/Audit, Insurance, Law), Energy, Travel and Leisure, and Relocation.
exhibits.data: Y-axis: 0 to 60 MM nights; five years of bars (2006-2010) for each of the four segments; exact bar heights not labeled but trends are visible.

exhibits.title: Increasing penetration in current clients
exhibits.shows: A table listing four growth options with their up-front program cost and projected revenue impact under a good economy versus a bad economy.
exhibits.data: Rewards/Points Program: $50M cost | Good: 5% revenue increase with existing customers | Bad: 1% revenue increase with existing customers. Advertising Campaign: $100M cost | Good: 10% revenue increase | Bad: no effect. Hire Key Account Representatives: $1MM cost | Good: 1% revenue increase | Bad: 1% revenue increase. Create Special Sales Force Incentives: $10MM cost | Good: 10% revenue increase | Bad: 5% decrease in revenue with existing customers.

framework: Understand current revenue baseline: total nights stayed, revenue per night, and cost per night
Analyze existing customer mix by industry (Exhibit 1): identify growth and declining segments and potential new industries
Evaluate options to increase penetration with existing customers (Exhibit 2): compare expected profitability under different economic scenarios
Consider new customer acquisition: identify untapped industries where corporate housing could be marketed
Synthesize findings and recommend the optimal growth path, considering risk profile and capital constraints

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 1, what trends do you observe in Arbor's mix of clients? What percentage of 2008 nights stayed/revenue comes from Professional Services?
questions.guidance: Candidate should observe: Professional Services declined in 2008-2009 (likely due to economic slowdown reducing consulting/audit projects) but recovered in 2010. Energy has remained steady (longer-term projects, less fluctuation). Travel & Leisure decreased (tied to disposable income). Relocation steadily increased (people moving to find new jobs). For the math: Professional Services accounts for approximately 40% of 2008 nights stayed. Candidate should also brainstorm industries not represented (Government, Education/Higher Ed, Entertainment/TV & Movies, Construction, Healthcare).

math.setup: What percentage of 2008 total nights stayed comes from Professional Services?
steps: Read Professional Services bar for 2008 from Exhibit 1: approximately 40 MM nights
Read total nights stayed in 2008 across all four segments: approximately 100 MM nights

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2, which growth option should Arbor pursue to maximize penetration with existing customers? Assume 100MM nights stayed in 2010, each night is worth $200 in revenue and costs $150 (so $50 contribution margin). There is a 50% probability of a good economy and 50% probability of a bad economy.
questions.guidance: Candidate should compute expected profit for each option using the formula: Expected Profit = (Good outcome contribution * 50%) + (Bad outcome contribution * 50%) - Up-front cost. Strong candidates note: Ad Campaign has highest expected return but also highest variance (50% chance of no benefit and $100MM sunk). Key Account Reps is the safest with no downside risk. Special Incentives is the riskiest (potential $250MM contribution loss). Recommendation depends on risk profile: risk-neutral -> Advertising Campaign; risk-averse -> Key Account Representatives; capital-constrained -> Rewards or Key Accounts.

math.setup: Base: 100MM nights stayed in 2010; Revenue/night = $200; Cost/night = $150; Contribution/night = $50. A 1% increase = 1MM nights = $200MM revenue = $50MM contribution. Economy: 50% good, 50% bad.
steps: Rewards/Points Program: Good = 5% increase = 5MM nights = $250MM contribution; Bad = 1% increase = 1MM nights = $50MM contribution. Expected = (250*50% + 50*50%) - 50 cost = 125 + 25 - 50 = $100MM expected profit.
Advertising Campaign: Good = 10% increase = 10MM nights = $500MM contribution; Bad = no effect = $0. Expected = (500*50% + 0*50%) - 100 cost = 250 + 0 - 100 = $150MM expected profit.
Hire Key Account Representatives: Good = 1% increase = $50MM contribution; Bad = 1% increase = $50MM contribution. Expected = (50*50% + 50*50%) - 1 cost = 25 + 25 - 1 = $49MM expected profit.

Special Sales Force Incentives: Good = 10% increase = $500MM contribution; Bad = 5% decrease = -$250MM contribution. Expected = (500*50% + (-250)*50%) - 10 cost = 250 - 125 - 10 = $115MM expected profit (note: original casebook states $100MM; some rounding may apply given the $25MM vs $10MM cost discrepancy between exhibits).
math.answer: Expected profits: Advertising Campaign $150MM > Special Incentives ~$115MM > Rewards $100MM > Key Account Reps $49MM. Risk-neutral choice: Advertising Campaign. Risk-averse choice: Key Account Representatives (guaranteed positive return, minimal cost).

brainstorming.prompt: What new industries or customer segments, not currently represented in Exhibit 1, could Arbor Housing target to grow its customer base?

categories.name: Entertainment & Media
ideas: Film and TV production crews on location
Sports teams during away seasons or training camps

categories.name: Healthcare
ideas: Traveling nurses and locum tenens physicians

recommendation: Arbor Housing should launch an Advertising Campaign to increase penetration with existing customers, as it offers the highest expected profit ($150MM) under risk-neutral assumptions
Simultaneously, Arbor should pursue new industry verticals — particularly Government, Healthcare, and Entertainment — to diversify revenue and reduce dependency on Professional Services cycles
risks: The Advertising Campaign has a 50% chance of no return, resulting in a $100MM loss if the economy is bad
Heavy reliance on Professional Services (40% of revenue in 2008) creates cyclical vulnerability
Expanding into new industries requires building new sales relationships and may take time to generate revenue
next_steps: Assess Arbor's risk tolerance and capital availability with the PE firm to confirm Advertising Campaign feasibility
Conduct market sizing of target new industries (Government, Healthcare, Entertainment) to prioritize entry
Pilot Key Account Representatives in the highest-value new verticals as a low-risk complement to the Advertising Campaign
